extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners designing or analyzing algorithms for conference/online peer-review systems (ML/algorithms/operations-research audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating algorithms that choose an ordering of papers to present to arriving reviewers (for bidding/selection) to maximize a combined objective of paper-side utility and reviewer-side utility, conditioned on past bids and similarity scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected total gain objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximize the expected combined gain from a reviewer: the sum over papers of expected paper-side gain γ_p(gn−1,j + bid) plus λ times the reviewer-side gain γ_r(π(j), S), with expectation taken over random bids and conditioned on the history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formally maximize E[∑_j γ_p(gn−1,j + b_{n,j}) | H_{n−1}] + λ ∑_j γ_r(π_n(j), S_{n,j}); use this immediate expected gain as the optimization objective for ordering papers shown to a reviewer. The objective explicitly trades off paper-side benefit (diminishing returns on bids) and reviewer-side benefit via the scalar λ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper-side gain properties (γ_p)
rubrics_metrics.description: γ_p is a paper-side gain function that is increasing in number of bids and exhibits diminishing returns (concavity). Example used in proofs: γ_p(x) = √x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions hinge on marginal gains Δγ_p(·) = γ_p(g+1) − γ_p(g). The diminishing-returns property makes placing items with fewer prior bids earlier potentially more valuable for paper-side gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer-side gain properties (γ_r)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer-side gain depends on paper position and similarity score; it increases with similarity and typically decreases with worse (later) positions via a position-dependent factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the paper γ_r is decomposed (example) as γ_r(π, S) = (2S − 1) f_π(π). Thus higher similarity and better positions yield higher reviewer-side gain; ordering should account for both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidding probability model (f) and decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The bidding probability f(π, S) decomposes multiplicatively into a similarity-dependent term and a position-dependent term: f(π, S) = S · f_π(π), where f_π(π) is decreasing in position (example f_π(π) = 1 / log2(π + 1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decomposition is used to compute expected paper-side gains and to derive weights for assignment. Position dependence (decreasing f_π) captures user attention/position bias; similarity scales the baseline probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering as linear sum assignment (tractable optimization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The optimal ordering for a reviewer that maximizes immediate expected gain can be formulated as a linear sum assignment problem: choose x_{j,k} binary indicators (paper j shown at position k) to maximize ∑_{j,k} w_{j,k} x_{j,k} subject to permutation constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weights are w_{j,k} = f(k, S_{i,j})(γ_p(g_{i−1,j}+1) − γ_p(g_{i−1,j})) + λ γ_r(k, S_{i,j}). Because the assignment constraint matrix is totally unimodular, the integer constraints can be relaxed and solved as an LP to obtain an integral optimal ordering efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local optimality criterion for SUPER*
rubrics_metrics.description: SUPER* selects the paper ordering that maximizes the immediate expected gain conditioned on history (using the assignment formulation). With zero heuristic (h_i,j = 0) this makes SUPER* locally optimal for any arriving reviewer; for the final reviewer SUPER* is optimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement Algorithm 2: compute weights w_{j,k} (including heuristic if present) and solve the linear assignment LP to obtain ordering. Local optimality means SUPER* maximizes the immediate expected gain given current information, though it may not be globally optimal over future arrivals unless heuristics capture future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic incorporation (h_{i,j}) and zero-heuristic interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: A heuristic h_{i,j} estimates the expected number of future bids on paper j at arrival of reviewer i. SUPER* uses h_{i,j} in weights: γ_p(g_{i−1,j} + h_{i,j} + 1) − γ_p(g_{i−1,j} + h_{i,j}). If h_{i,j} = 0 (zero heuristic), SUPER* optimizes immediate expected gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use non-zero heuristics to incorporate anticipated future information; if no reliable heuristic exists, zero heuristic yields locally optimal immediate decisions. Heuristics allow adapting to changing action sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline algorithms and their evaluation dimensions (SIM, BID, RAND)
rubrics_metrics.description: SIM orders papers by decreasing similarity scores (optimizes reviewer-side gain only); BID orders by current number of bids; RAND orders uniformly at random.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or comparing algorithms, analyze both paper-side and reviewer-side components; SIM attains maximal expected reviewer-side gain but can be arbitrarily suboptimal for the combined objective because it ignores prior bid counts and diminishing returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of history H_{i−1} in decision making
rubrics_metrics.description: History H_{i−1} is defined as the information available when reviewer i arrives (previous bids and the orderings shown to previous reviewers). Decisions (orderings) should be conditioned on this history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All expectations and weight computations (γ_p, f, etc.) are computed conditioned on H_{i−1}; treat prior bid counts g_{i−1,j} as deterministic given H_{i−1} when computing immediate expected gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie-breaking determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: To make algorithmic orderings non-random in analysis, assume a deterministic tie-breaking mechanism (e.g., break ties by paper index j < j').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption simplifies theoretical comparison and ensures SUPER* produces a non-random ordering given deterministic ties; implementation may use any consistent tie-breaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic decomposition for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: For theoretical comparison, decompose expected gain into paper-side and reviewer-side components and compare these per-algorithm under the same history; derive α_{i,j}-style weights (α_{n,j} = S_{n,j}(Δγ_p) + λ(2S_{n,j} − 1)) to identify ordering structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decomposition lets one reason about optimal orderings as sorting by α-values because f_π is monotone; use such decompositions to construct worst-case instances and to prove suboptimality bounds for baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worst-case instance construction for baseline suboptimality
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate robustness, construct problem instances where similarity scores are nearly equal but prior bid counts differ markedly; due to diminishing returns, presenting low-bid papers earlier yields better paper-side gains, which SIM (similarity-only) may miss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design worst-case instances (e.g., half papers with one prior bid, half with zero; similarity differences tiny) to prove lower bounds on performance gaps between SUPER* and baselines; include both paper-side and reviewer-side contributions when measuring regret.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutation constraints for valid orderings
rubrics_metrics.description: Orderings are permutations: each paper must be assigned to exactly one position and each position must have exactly one paper (constraints ∑_k x_{j,k} = 1 for all j and ∑_j x_{j,k} = 1 for all k with x_{j,k} ∈ {0,1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate ordering problems as assignment problems respecting permutation constraints; use LP relaxation justified by total unimodularity to solve efficiently.
